summary.text: The strongest convergent signal in ulcerative colitis mucosa is the neutrophil chemokine axis. CXCR2 leads the convergence ranking: it is up in all eight cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.814]), has Open Targets genetic support and has clinical-stage antagonists in other indications. But single-cell data place almost all of its transcripts in neutrophils (share [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]), and only a small change remains after composition adjustment ([gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4409]). The axis is therefore best read as neutrophil recruitment: a druggable but unapproved UC target and a strong marker of neutrophil influx.

Behind the neutrophil signal, several changes are intrinsic to the tissue and survive composition adjustment. The epithelium loses its metabolic and absorptive programme: HMGCS2 falls in all eight cohorts (pooled [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.838]) and its protein is lost in an independent proteomics study ([gene=HMGCS2; type=proteomics_de; source=DATASET:PROTEOMICS_SCHNIERS2019; contrast=inflamed UC at diagnosis vs healthy colon mucosa; log2_ratio=-3.094]), while the epithelial oxidase DUOX2 rises. Resident myeloid cells raise IDO1 (adjusted [gene=IDO1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8505]), and inflammatory fibroblasts raise MMP1 (adjusted [gene=MMP1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.2636]) and CHI3L1. These are the candidates that point at a cell type rather than at cell influx.

Genetics separates causes from consequences. The approved-target positive control IL12B has the strongest plasma Mendelian randomisation in the screen, with higher protein raising UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]); it colocalises and replicates in FinnGen, which supports the design. In contrast, genetically higher plasma PD-L1 is protective (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]) although CD274 is up in mucosa, so inhibiting PD-L1 would be the wrong direction. CXCL8, one of the largest expression changes, has a null plasma MR (p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]). CXCR2 itself has no cis instrument and could not be tested.

Baseline biopsies do not yet give drug-specific stratifiers. Higher CXCR2 predicts ustekinumab non-response (BH padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=9.69e-6]), but the same association appears in UNIFI placebo (padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0126]). OSM, TREM1, CXCL8 and TNFa pathway activity follow the same pattern, so these genes mark disease severity rather than resistance to one drug, and the drug targets IL23A and ITGB7 do not stratify response to their own drugs.

Among first-in-class candidates without a drug, the fibroblast-derived CHRDL2 and the epithelial XKR9 are the leading hypotheses for experimental validation. Both lack genetic and functional evidence. CHRDL2 is largely a fibroblast-expansion signal, and XKR9 is the only intrinsic candidate but replicates in only a subset of cohorts.

expression.text: The meta-analysis across eight cohorts gives a consistent picture of inflamed UC mucosa. The largest and most reproducible increases are antimicrobial, neutrophil and tissue-injury genes, each up in all eight cohorts: CHI3L1 (pooled log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.875]), MMP3 ([gene=MMP3; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.901]), the calprotectin component S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.77]), the epithelial oxidase DUOX2 ([gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.412]), the neutrophil chemokine CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.864]) and the interferon-induced IDO1 ([gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.118]). MMP1, MMP7 and MMP10 follow MMP3, and S100A9 and S100A12 follow S100A8. Together they describe a mucosa flooded with neutrophils and myeloid cells, remodelling its matrix and producing reactive oxygen and antimicrobial proteins.

The decreases are just as strong and point to loss of differentiated colonocyte function. AQP8 shows the largest pooled decrease ([gene=AQP8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-5.246]), and the ketogenesis enzyme HMGCS2 is down in all eight cohorts ([gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.838]). The chloride/bicarbonate exchanger SLC26A3, a UC genetic locus, is also down in all eight cohorts ([gene=SLC26A3; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-1.702]). CLDN8, PCK1, GUCA2A/B, SLC26A2 and ADH1C belong to the same lost absorptive and metabolic signature. This is the epithelial-metabolism loss of active UC: these genes are good activity biomarkers, and for SLC26A3 restoration rather than inhibition would be the therapeutic logic.

Several highly ranked genes owe their rank to genetics and tractability rather than to the size of their expression change. JAK2 rises only modestly though consistently (pooled [gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.874]), and CD274 (PD-L1) shows a moderate increase ([gene=CD274; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=1.974]) that most likely reflects interferon-driven induction and immune-cell influx. The direction of the top changes is consistent across cohorts, but their size is not: pooled heterogeneity is very high, driven by platform differences and compressed microarray fold changes.

inflammation.text: Comparing inflamed with non-inflamed mucosa from the same patients shows that the neutrophil signal is local. CXCR2 is clearly higher in inflamed than in paired non-inflamed tissue (log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972]), while non-inflamed mucosa shows only a small rise over controls ([gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.6399]). It therefore marks active inflammation rather than a constitutive trait of UC mucosa.

The epithelial metabolic loss is also confined to inflamed tissue. HMGCS2 is unchanged in non-inflamed UC mucosa ([gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-0.0649]) despite its strong pooled loss, so it reports local injury rather than a field defect present before inflammation, and the change survives covariate adjustment.

replication.text: Replication is the strongest feature of the leading genes. CXCR2, CXCL8, IDO1, CHI3L1, MMP3, DUOX2, S100A8 and HMGCS2 change in the same direction in the discovery cohort and in all four microarray and three RNA-seq replication cohorts, and CXCL8 holds after adjustment for colon segment, age and sex ([gene=CXCL8; type=expression_adjusted; source=DATASET:GSE193677; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed UC vs control, biopsy level; adjusted_log2fc=2.499]). CXCR1 replicates in most but not all cohorts. At protein level, the independent proteomics study confirms the loss of HMGCS2 ([gene=HMGCS2; type=proteomics_de; source=DATASET:PROTEOMICS_SCHNIERS2019; contrast=inflamed UC at diagnosis vs healthy colon mucosa; log2_ratio=-3.094]) and the rise of IDO1 ([gene=IDO1; type=proteomics_de; source=DATASET:PROTEOMICS_SCHNIERS2019; contrast=inflamed UC at diagnosis vs healthy colon mucosa; log2_ratio=0.917]). The CHI3L1 protein rise is much smaller than its RNA change ([gene=CHI3L1; type=proteomics_de; source=DATASET:PROTEOMICS_SCHNIERS2019; contrast=inflamed UC at diagnosis vs healthy colon mucosa; log2_ratio=0.607]) and was not called significant by the study authors. Proteomics covers only a subset of genes, and an unmeasured gene is not evidence against it.

literature.text: Published support is thinnest where the convergence score is highest. CXCR2 has no verbatim-checked literature relations in the graph. Its corpus support is indirect: a title-level report naming CXCR1 and CXCR2 as neutrophil extracellular trap-related treatment targets in UC, a CXCL5/CXCR2 eQTL and pQTL study, a report that C/EBPbeta drives CXCR2 ligands to recruit neutrophils, and machine-extracted PubTator3 associations. No UC trial of a CXCR2 antagonist appears in the corpus. Mechanistic literature exists for a few other leading genes but comes from single studies. In one, IDO1 drove M1 macrophage polarisation through the GRP78-XBP1 stress pathway and an IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis. In another, AQP9 promoted neutrophil extracellular trap formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis, which again places the AQP9 signal in infiltrating neutrophils rather than epithelium.

Most gene-level literature is diagnostic or bioinformatic. MMP1, MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B correlated with endoscopic and histological indices in mirikizumab trial transcriptomics, and MMP10 was reported up before diagnosis, in active versus remitting UC, and as a credible diagnostic biomarker together with CXCL1 and DUOX2. S100A9 had excellent performance for active UC, and tofacitinib response was associated with its fall in resident macrophages. Down-regulated SLC26A2 and HMGCS2 had diagnostic value and tracked Mayo score and PUCAI. CHI3L1 promoted macrophage pyroptosis through a BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis, and a herbal formula alleviated colitis by inhibiting DUOX2 overexpression. A review places the CXCL8-CXCR1/CXCR2 axis upstream of PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signalling. LCN2 tracked disease duration and colitis-associated cancer, and CD274 was named a hub gene linked to macrophage infiltration and validated by immunohistochemistry. These are mostly single-study or in-silico results, with few prospective validations.

external.text: Approved UC target classes behave as positive controls. IL12B, the p40 subunit targeted by ustekinumab, has the strongest plasma MR in the screen (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]), colocalises with the IBD GWAS signal and replicates in FinnGen and Liu 2023, so genetics supports inhibition. JAK2 has a high Open Targets association (score [gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318]) but only a small expression change and no MR instrument. The expression-led candidates have no approved UC drug. CXCR2 has strong Open Targets genetic association ([gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.8171]) and antagonists from other indications (reparixin at phase 3, navarixin, ladarixin and SX-682 at phase 2). It is not loss-of-function constrained and has no curated safety events. It lacks a cis-pQTL or gut eQTL instrument, which is not evidence against it, and mouse literature reports a CXCR2 antagonist ameliorating acute colitis, without a curated MGI colitis phenotype. MMP1 and the other MMPs, IDO1 and CHI3L1 have strong expression but no UC genetic association, while SLC26A3 is the one down-regulated epithelial gene with genetic support.

Mendelian randomisation exposes direction conflicts. Genetically higher plasma PD-L1 lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]); the signal colocalises with an IBD GWAS signal and replicates in FinnGen (OR [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; finngen_odds_ratio_per_sd=0.734]), with nominal heterogeneity across its three instruments (p [gene=CD274; type=mr_sensitivity; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; layer=plasma_protein; heterogeneity_p=0.0259]). The mucosal rise of CD274 is therefore probably protective feedback. CXCL5 is likewise up in biopsies but genetically protective (OR per SD [gene=CXCL5; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.634]); it does not colocalise, so a neighbouring variant in the CXCL cluster cannot be excluded. The plasma MR is null for CXCL8 (p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]), IDO1 (p [gene=IDO1; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.111]) and FCGR2A (p [gene=FCGR2A; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.68]), and the IDO1 colon eQTL and the FCGR2A gut single-cell eQTL are also not significant. Gut-tissue MR highlights different loci: IRF8 in transverse colon raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IRF8; type=mendelian_randomization_gut; source=DATASET:MR_GUT_EQTL_UC; layer=colon_tissue; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.937]) and colocalises with a single instrument, alongside IRF5, GSDMB and INAVA. The blood and gut layers rarely test the same genes, so their agreement cannot be judged for the leading candidates.

cells.text: The single-cell data split the leading genes into markers of neutrophil influx and changes within resident cells. Neutrophils make most of the inflamed-mucosa transcripts of CXCR2 (share [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]), CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.873]) and S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.909]); CXCR1 and AQP9 follow the same pattern. After composition adjustment, CXCL8 is no longer significant (padj [gene=CXCL8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.0523]), and CXCR2 keeps only a small change (adjusted [gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4409]), as do CXCR1 ([gene=CXCR1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.5702]), AQP9 ([gene=AQP9; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8551]) and S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.9231]). These are markers of neutrophil recruitment. Targeting CXCR2 or CXCR1 means blocking neutrophil arrival rather than correcting a tissue programme. The attribution of CXCR2 does not replicate: Smillie 2019 has no neutrophils and assigns it to T/NK cells, and the second dataset points to myeloid cells.

Other leading genes are made by resident cells and keep a large change after adjustment. IDO1 comes from macrophages and DC1, replicated in the second dataset, with a small neutrophil share ([gene=IDO1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.072]), and stays clearly changed after adjustment ([gene=IDO1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8505]). DUOX2 is epithelial ([gene=DUOX2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.947]) with a retained change ([gene=DUOX2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3161]). MMP1 and CHI3L1 come from inflammatory fibroblasts, replicated in the second dataset (CHI3L1 lineage share [gene=CHI3L1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.941]), and both keep large adjusted changes (MMP1 [gene=MMP1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.2636], CHI3L1 [gene=CHI3L1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3967]), although neutrophils also contribute part of the CHI3L1 signal. These are the candidates with a defined producing cell: myeloid IDO1, epithelial DUOX2 and fibroblast MMP1 and CHI3L1.

CD274 sits in between: its myeloid attribution replicates, but neutrophil states carry much of it ([gene=CD274; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.687]), and a significant change remains after adjustment ([gene=CD274; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4978]). The adjustment can over-correct, because lineage scores also rise when resident cells activate. A lost signal such as CXCL8 is therefore not proof of pure influx, while a retained one is strong evidence of a tissue change.

spatial.text: In situ evidence is available only for MMP1. In the deconvolved Visium spots, inflammatory fibroblasts explain most of its signal (contribution [gene=MMP1; type=spatial_visium_cell; source=DATASET:GSE189184; in_situ_contribution=0.579]), which agrees with the single-cell attribution to inflammatory fibroblasts. CosMx detects MMP1 only at background, so the tissue-level and single-cell spatial views do not yet agree, and the attribution has no in situ confirmation at single-cell resolution. The other leading candidates were not tested in situ.

pathways.text: Inflamed mucosa activates nearly every inflammatory pathway at once. NF-kB activity is raised in all eight cohorts, strongest in GSE206285 (t [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=18.79]). TNFa, JAK-STAT, MAPK, PI3K, TGFb, EGFR and hypoxia are also up in all eight cohorts, with no cohort going down. Among transcription factors, inferred STAT3 activity is up in all eight cohorts, peaking in GSE206285 (t [type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=24.0]), as is AP1. The TNF and JAK-STAT axes are therefore active and already drug-targeted. But this broad activation is shared by all inflamed samples and does not discriminate between candidates. Not every pathway rises: p53 is down in a minority of cohorts and up in none, and androgen, TRAIL, VEGF and estrogen are inconsistent.

The most specific cell-cell circuit is neutrophil-to-neutrophil. The CXCR4-high neutrophil state sends CXCL8 to CXCR2 on the generic neutrophil state, with a large rise over uninflamed tissue (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.755]), and OSM-high and PADI4-high neutrophils also act as CXCR2 receivers. Neutrophil CXCL8 also reaches ACKR1 on venular endothelium (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=1.991]). Because ACKR1 is an atypical receptor, this is chemokine presentation and leukocyte trafficking rather than classical signalling. IL1B is sent mainly by monocyte-derived macrophages to neutrophil states through IL1R2 (log2 change to the PADI4-high state [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=1.168]). IL1R2 is mostly a decoy receptor, so the top IL1B pairs may not be activating. These scores are co-expression in one single-cell dataset, not proof of signalling.

Separating targeted from untargeted axes: TNF, JAK-STAT and IL-23 are already treated in UC. The CXCL8-CXCR1/CXCR2 circuit is druggable, with dual antagonists and anti-IL-8 antibodies, but untargeted in UC. TREM1, a myeloid receptor up in all eight cohorts, has only the phase 2 peptide nangibotide and no genetic support. The MMP stromal-remodelling arm (MMP1, MMP3, MMP7, MMP10) remains untargeted after broad MMP inhibitors failed for toxicity and specificity. IDO1 inhibitors exist from oncology, but their direction in UC is unclear, because IDO1 is probably an interferon-induced counter-regulatory gene.

treatment.text: Baseline pathway activity tracks severity rather than resistance to a specific drug. TNFa activity is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000484]) but also in UNIFI placebo non-responders (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.00608]), while the small PURSUIT placebo arm shows nothing (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (PURSUIT).padj=0.932]). TGFb follows the same pattern (ustekinumab padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000493], UNIFI placebo padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.00984]). NF-kB activity is higher in infliximab non-responders (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.infliximab.padj=0.000294]) and in several other arms including placebo, but not in the PROTECT aminosalicylate arm (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.5-ASA (PROTECT).padj=0.414]). JAK-STAT is associated with ustekinumab non-response (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0124]) but not with golimumab (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.golimumab.padj=0.204]), so it is not a uniform anti-TNF resistance signal.

At gene level the pattern is the same. OSM is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000264]), but the drug-vs-placebo interaction is null (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; interaction.ustekinumab.padj=0.982]), the placebo trend runs the same way (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.116]), and nothing survives in golimumab, infliximab or vedolizumab. TREM1 (ustekinumab padj [gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000474]; placebo padj [gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0234]) and CXCL8 (ustekinumab padj [gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000102]; placebo padj [gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0154]) likewise mark severity. In the adalimumab single-cell atlas, CXCL8 shows no baseline difference between remitters and non-remitters. The drugs' own targets do not stratify response: baseline IL23A for ustekinumab (padj [gene=IL23A; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.977]) and ITGB7 for vedolizumab (padj [gene=ITGB7; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.vedolizumab.padj=0.995]). Response cohorts outside UNIFI are small, so these null results partly reflect low power.

discovery.text: CHRDL2 is the top first-in-class candidate from the discovery screen. It is antibody-tractable with no clinical drug, and its transcripts come mostly from inflammatory fibroblasts. Only a minority of its bulk signal is retained after composition correction (retained [gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.2764]), so much of it reflects fibroblast expansion. Its vital-organ RNA reaches [gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; vital_max_ntpm=42.6] nTPM, the highest of the group, which is a safety point to check. Genetic and functional evidence is missing. It is a hypothesis for testing whether fibroblast-derived CHRDL2 modulates BMP signalling in inflamed mucosa.

XKR9 is the only leading novel candidate classed as intrinsic: it is epithelial, and most of its change survives composition correction (retained [gene=XKR9; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.7976]). But it is up in only a subset of cohorts and only a small fraction of cells express it, so its replication is weaker than that of the convergence leaders. Validation would need protein detection in epithelium and replication in further cohorts before any tractability work.

CPXM1 is a stromal fibroblast candidate whose cell attribution replicates in a second single-cell dataset. Less than half of its change is retained after adjustment ([gene=CPXM1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.4136]), so it is partly a fibroblast-expansion signal. Its vital-organ expression is low, but there is no genetic or mechanistic evidence for it.

LAX1 is a negative result of the screen. Despite very low vital-organ expression, it is made mainly by plasma and T cells, its lineage does not replicate in the second dataset, and only a small share survives composition correction (retained [gene=LAX1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.23]). It most likely reflects lymphocyte infiltration rather than a tissue change and is not a first-in-class target.

integration.text: The streams agree on the neutrophil axis and on the approved positive controls. CXCR2 converges across expression, replication, paired inflammation, Open Targets genetics and tractability, and the pathway stream finds the CXCL8-CXCR2 neutrophil circuit to be the most specific cell-cell signal. The IL12B positive control is supported by both plasma MR and Open Targets, and the JAK-STAT and TNF pathways are active in all cohorts, consistent with the approved drug classes. Expression, single-cell data and proteomics agree that HMGCS2 and the absorptive epithelial programme are lost locally in inflamed tissue.

The streams disagree in three places. First, the cell and treatment streams downgrade the top of the ranking. The CXCR2 and CXCL8 bulk signals are largely neutrophil influx, and their association with poor response is mirrored in placebo, so they mark severity. Second, genetics contradicts expression for CD274 and CXCL5, both up in mucosa but genetically protective, while the CXCL8 MR is null despite one of the largest expression changes. Third, the tissue-intrinsic candidates with a clear producing cell (IDO1, DUOX2, MMP1, CHI3L1) lack genetic support, and the genetically supported JAK2 and gut-eQTL loci such as IRF8 barely move in expression. The literature stream is thin for the top genes, with no verbatim-checked relations for CXCR2 or CD274.

targets.rationale: Ranks first on convergence: up in all eight cohorts and locally in inflamed mucosa, with strong Open Targets genetic association and clinical-stage dual CXCR1/CXCR2 antagonists in other indications. Kept first, but as a neutrophil-recruitment target rather than a tissue target: neutrophils make most of its transcripts, little change survives composition adjustment, no MR instrument exists, and its link to poor ustekinumab response is mirrored in placebo, so it also marks severity.

Positive control: the approved ustekinumab target has the strongest plasma MR in the screen, with higher protein raising UC risk, colocalisation with the IBD GWAS signal and FinnGen replication. Placed above the expression-led genes because it has causal genetic support, although it is not in the top of the expression ranking.

Positive control for the approved JAK-inhibitor class: high Open Targets genetic association and JAK-STAT activity up in every cohort, despite only a modest mRNA change. Its rank comes from genetics and tractability, not from expression, and it has no MR instrument.

Up in all eight cohorts and at protein level, produced by resident macrophages and DC1, and still changed after composition adjustment, so it is a genuine tissue change. A preclinical study found that IDO inhibition ameliorated colitis. It is ranked below the controls because plasma MR and colon eQTL are null and its therapeutic direction is uncertain: it may be counter-regulatory.

The second IL-8 receptor, rank two on convergence and shared with CXCR2 by the dual antagonists, so it is one druggable axis with CXCR2. Placed lower because it replicates in most but not all cohorts and, like CXCR2, it mostly tracks neutrophil arrival.

Strongly up in all eight cohorts, made by inflammatory fibroblasts with a large change retained after adjustment and Visium support for the fibroblast source. It has zero UC genetic association, broad MMP inhibitors have failed historically, and CosMx detects it only at background. It is best used as a stromal-remodelling biomarker and only exploratory as a target.

Epithelial reactive-oxygen gene, up in all eight cohorts with a tissue-intrinsic change after adjustment and literature naming it a credible diagnostic biomarker. A strong biomarker of epithelial inflammatory stress. It has no genetic support or drug, so it is not ranked as a target.

Among the largest RNA increases, made by inflammatory fibroblasts and retained after adjustment. The protein rise is much smaller and was not called significant by the proteomics authors, so it is a tissue biomarker. Target status awaits better protein and genetic evidence.

One of the largest and most reproducible increases and the ligand of the leading circuit. It is demoted from rank three to a biomarker because plasma MR is null, the change loses significance after composition adjustment, and its association with poor response is mirrored in placebo.

Epithelial ketogenesis enzyme lost in all eight cohorts and at protein level, unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa. It is a robust biomarker of local epithelial metabolic collapse, not an inhibitable target.

Up in all eight cohorts with genetic association, but genetically higher plasma PD-L1 is protective, with colocalisation and FinnGen replication. The rise is probably protective feedback, so PD-L1 blockade is contraindicated by the genetics. Listed as a biomarker and as a possible agonism hypothesis, not a target to inhibit.

The calprotectin component, up in all eight cohorts and made mostly by neutrophils, with only part of the change retained after adjustment. It is the tissue counterpart of an established faecal activity biomarker and serves as a positive control for the biomarker category.

Exploratory: the top first-in-class candidate from the discovery screen. It is antibody-tractable, has no drug and is made by inflammatory fibroblasts. It is partly a fibroblast-expansion signal, has the highest vital-organ expression of the group, and lacks genetic and functional evidence, so it needs experimental validation.

Exploratory: the only intrinsic epithelial novel candidate, with most of its change retained after composition correction. It is up in only a subset of cohorts and expressed by few cells, so replication and protein-level confirmation are needed first.

limitations.text: Bulk biopsies mix cell influx with tissue change. The composition adjustment that separates them can over-correct when resident cells activate, and the neutrophil attribution rests on one single-cell dataset (Gubatan) because Smillie captured no neutrophils.

Mendelian randomisation could not test CXCR2, CXCR1 or JAK2 (no cis instrument), and most gut-eQTL tests use a single instrument. Blood and gut layers rarely test the same genes, so absence of MR support is not evidence against these candidates.

Literature support for CXCR2, CD274 and JAK2 comes from title-level sentences, machine-extracted PubTator3 associations and Open Targets, not from verbatim-checked relations. Agent verification removed literature chunks that were not linked to CD274 and JAK2.

Spatial evidence covers only MMP1 (Visium deconvolution; CosMx at background). Xenium and spatial-neighbourhood analyses were not run for the other leading candidates. CXCL1, MMP3, IL1B and TREM1 have no composition-adjusted result.

Treatment-response cohorts outside UNIFI are small, and the PURSUIT placebo arm is tiny, so null results for golimumab, infliximab and vedolizumab partly reflect low power. All associations are baseline and observational.

Pathway and transcription-factor activities are inferred from bulk transcriptomes and rise together in inflamed mucosa. Ligand-receptor scores are co-expression in one dataset, and no neutrophil-to-fibroblast circuit (such as OSM to inflammatory fibroblasts) was tested.

Pooled heterogeneity is very high for nearly all top genes because of platform differences, so the direction of change is robust but its size is not. Mouse evidence is literature counts only, without curated MGI colitis phenotypes for the leading genes.

Before agent verification, specialist statements were edited only in form: unbound small integers were written as words, pathway-level findings lost a gene label that was not a gene, and numbers printed beside their annotations were removed. No values or interpretations were changed.
